quote: 16.5 Disclaimer of Liability for Consequential Damages. UNLESS EXPRESSLY PROVIDED HEREUNDER, IN NO EVENT SHALL EITHER PARTY OR ANY OF ITS RESPECTIVE AFFILIATES AND THEIR RESPECTIVE OFFICERS, DIRECTORS AND EMPLOYEES BE LIABLE UNDER THIS AGREEMENT FOR SPECIAL, INDIRECT, PUNITIVE, INCIDENTAL OR CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES SUFFERED BY THE OTHER PARTY UNDER THIS AGREEMENT
rationale: Section 16.5 is the only limitation-of-liability provision in the Agreement: it is a mutual exclusion of special, indirect, punitive, incidental and consequential damages, with carve-outs preserving third-party indemnity payments under Article 10 and Sections 16.1/16.2 and disapplying the limitation for gross negligence or willful misconduct. However, a document-wide search ("aggregate liability", "shall not exceed", "liable", "limitation of liability") returns no monetary cap of any kind — the only "shall not exceed" language is milestone/royalty mechanics in Article VI. Both parties therefore bear unlimited direct liability, including Ono's broad product-liability and Article 15 breach exposure. That fails even the fallback, which requires a mutual cap (12 months' fees) with carve-outs; the exclusion of consequential damages and the existing carve-outs are helpful but are not a cap. The clause is mutual, so this is not walk-away territory (Ono is not capped while Array is uncapped), and we have kept the edit to a single appended sentence in 16.5 rather than restructuring Article 16: a mutual cap at the greater of twelve months' payments by Ono and USD 1,000,000, with indemnification, confidentiality/data protection, gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement outside the cap (mirroring the existing 16.5 carve-outs) and Ono's payment obligations excluded from the cap basis.

quote: 18.9 Assignment. This Agreement may not be assigned by either Party to any Third Party without the written consent of the other Party hereto; except either Party may assign this Agreement without the other Party's consent to an entity that acquires substantially all of the business or assets of the assigning Party, whether by merger, acquisition or otherwise; provided that the acquiring party agrees in a writing delivered to the non-assigning Party to assume all of the rights and obligations of the assigning Party under this Agreement.
rationale: Section 18.9 is mutual and gives Ono the M&A carve-out we require: either Party may assign without consent to an entity acquiring substantially all of its business or assets by merger or acquisition, and any other assignment requires consent of the other Party. Affiliate assignment (18.9, second paragraph) is permitted with consent that "shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed", so the clause sits at the fallback position (mutual successor assignment plus a reasonableness standard for other assignments) rather than the preferred consent-free affiliate right; the narrow proviso allowing consent to be withheld where the assignment would create material adverse tax consequences is mutual and does not defeat the fallback. Change in Control mechanics run only against Array: Section 18.10 imposes firewall obligations on an Array Acquirer, and Section 4.5(b) (p0322) terminates on a Change in Control of Array — there is no Array right to terminate, re-price or restrict on a Change in Control of Ono, and no "deemed assignment" trigger. Minor shortfalls from preferred (no express bar on Array assigning to an Ono competitor, consent needed for Affiliate assignments) are noted but not redlined.

rationale: Ownership is otherwise sound for us: Section 11.1(a) leaves Ono owning IP made solely by Ono personnel, Section 2.6's Grant-Back is only a non-exclusive, Product-limited licence (no assignment of Ono IP or Improvements), Sections 4.7-4.8 exchange Data by licence/right of reference rather than transfer, Ono owns its INDs and Marketing Approvals (4.2(b)-(c)), and Article XII has Array assigning Product Trademarks to Ono. The failure is Section 11.1(c)-(d): jointly-created inventions are jointly owned, and 11.1(d) then confines each Party to internal-purpose practice and bars licensing, enforcement or assignment without the other's consent, save where the joint IP happens to fall within the licences granted (for Ono, only Products in the Ono Territory). That is joint ownership without an unrestricted right to exploit, which the playbook treats as walk-away territory, so it fails the fallback. The redline keeps the collaboration's joint-ownership architecture (deleting it outright would be disproportionate here) but restores an unrestricted right to practise, exploit and license co-owned IP, subject to the exclusive licences already granted, while retaining a consent gate on assigning a co-ownership interest.

quote: The seat of the arbitration shall be in Osaka, Japan, if it is demanded by Array, and in New York, NY, USA, if it is demanded by Ono, with hearings to held in the same location.
rationale: Section 18.3 selects the substantive law of the State of New York (conflicts principles excluded, CISG excluded), which is the playbook's preferred governing law. On forum, Article XVII routes disputes first to Senior Executives under Section 17.1 (45-day escalation), then to expert determination for JDRC/JCC-type "Expert Disputes" (17.2), and otherwise to mandatory ICC arbitration in three-member panels (17.3). The forum mechanic is arbitration rather than the New York County courts contemplated by the preferred position, but the material adverse features the rule targets are absent: there is no counterparty-home venue and no foreign seat imposed on us. The seat is New York when Ono demands arbitration and Osaka, Japan — our own home jurisdiction — when Array demands it, so the respondent-forum split runs in our favour on both branches; proceedings are in English, punitive damages are excluded, and each Party retains access to any court of competent jurisdiction for interim and conservatory relief (17.3(g)). Redlining to exclusive New York court jurisdiction would surrender our Osaka home-seat protection, so we do not flag it. Noted for the file only: arbitration in place of courts, and the carve-out allowing inventorship disputes to be pursued in any forum.

ops.text: (b) Return of Ono Data and Confidential Information; Transition Assistance. Upon the expiration or termination of this Agreement for any reason, (i) at Ono's request, Array shall provide reasonable transition assistance to Ono, its Affiliates and its designees for a period of up to six (6) months following the effective date of such expiration or termination, at Array's then-current rates; (ii) within thirty (30) days after Ono's written request, Array shall return to Ono all Data and Confidential Information of Ono then in Array's possession or control, in a commonly used, machine-readable format, excluding any Data or Ono Know-How that Array is expressly licensed or otherwise entitled to use or retain under this Agreement (including under Sections 14.2(a)(iii) and 14.2(a)(v)); and (iii) thereafter Array shall delete or destroy all such Data and Confidential Information of Ono from its systems and records, subject to Array's right to keep one (1) copy for archiving purposes, and shall certify such deletion or destruction to Ono in writing.

quote: (vi) Return of Materials. Within ninety (90) days after the end of the Wind-down Period, upon request by Array, Ono shall either deliver to Array or destroy all tangible items comprising, bearing or containing trademarks of Array (including the Product Trademarks), trade names, patents, copyrights, designs, drawings, formulas or other Data, photographs, samples, literature, sales and promotional aids ("Product Materials") and Confidential Information of Array, that is in Ono's possession, subject to Ono's right to keep one (1) copy for archiving purposes.

Article X contains no return/destruction provision at all (no "return or destroy" language exists elsewhere in the document), and nothing obliges Array to return, export or delete Ono's Data or Confidential Information, or to certify deletion. The only assistance obligation available to us is the mutual wind-down cooperation covenant in 14.2(a)(iv), which is directed at transitioning the Product back to Array rather than at supporting Ono, and is unconnected to any data return. With no data return or export obligation on the counterparty at all, the clause fails even the fallback (data export within 30 days) and sits in walk-away territory, so we propose inserting a reciprocal Section 14.2(b): up to six months' transition assistance at Array's then-current rates, return of our Data and Confidential Information within thirty days in machine-readable form, and certified deletion thereafter, carved back for the Data and Ono Know-How Array is expressly entitled to retain under 14.2(a)(iii) and (v) so the negotiated licence bargain is preserved.

verification.notes: The gap is real: 14.2(a)(iii), (iv) and (vi) impose one-way obligations on Ono (deliver Data/Ono Know-How, hand over customer data, return or destroy Array's Confidential Information and Product Materials), and no cited or referenced provision obliges Array to return, export, delete or certify deletion of Ono's Data or Confidential Information. With no data-return mechanic on the counterparty at all, the fallback (export within 30 days) is not met, so a 'missing' classification with an insert is the correct call rather than over-flagging an acceptable fallback. The redline is actionable and minimal in form: a single new reciprocal subsection placed at the end of Section 14.2 tracking the model language (up to 6 months' assistance at Array's then-current rates, return within 30 days in machine-readable format, then deletion with written certification), leaving all existing text untouched. The drafting respects the negotiated bargain: it expressly carves out Data and Ono Know-How Array is licensed or entitled to retain under 14.2(a)(iii) and (v), makes assistance elective ('at Ono's request') and paid, and mirrors the existing one-archival-copy concession in 14.2(a)(vi), so it does not reopen the licence grant or create an unbalanced obligation. Deterministic checks pass (operation applies; data-return/transition language present) and the comment is concise, first-person plural, cites the playbook position and offers the 90-day fallback. Minor points that do not defeat the finding: the comment's statement that nothing obliges Array 'to help us transition' slightly overstates matters given the mutual cooperation covenant in 14.2(a)(iv) (the rationale correctly acknowledges it and explains why it is inadequate), and the rule's detection guidance is framed for services/hosting agreements, so applying it to a pharma licence is a stretch — but the substantive reciprocity gap on return of our Data and Confidential Information is genuine. Residual drafting risk to confirm on execution: the insertion assumes Section 14.2 does not already contain a subsection (b) (the anchor paragraph p0667 was not included in the supplied original paragraphs), so the sub-numbering should be verified against the full Section 14.2.

ops.text: 9.7 Materials Warranty. Array warrants that all Materials supplied by or on behalf of Array to Ono under this Agreement will, at the time of delivery and through the expiration of the applicable shelf life or retest date, (a) conform in all material respects to the applicable product specifications and the certificate of analysis for the relevant batch, and (b) have been Manufactured in accordance with GMP and all other applicable Law. Array further warrants that it shall perform its obligations under this Agreement in a professional and workmanlike manner consistent with industry standards. For any Materials that fail to conform to the foregoing warranty, Array shall, at Ono's election, promptly replace such Materials at no additional cost to Ono or refund the amounts paid by Ono for such Materials, in each case together with any shipping, handling and destruction costs incurred by Ono.

quote: 15.4 Except as otherwise expressly set forth in this Agreement, neither Party makes any representation or extends any warranties of any kind either express or implied, including, but not limited to, warranties of merchantability, fitness for a particular purpose, noninfringement or validity of any patents issued or pending

Article IX merely defers specifications and "customary terms" to future clinical and commercial supply agreements (p0501, p0510), which leaves Ono with no conformance warranty under this Agreement. Combined with the broad implied-warranty disclaimer in 15.4 (which does carve out express terms, so it does not swallow anything, but there is nothing left to carve out), the deal falls below even the fallback position of a conformance warranty with a real remedy. We therefore propose a new Section 9.7 warranting that Materials conform to specifications and were Manufactured in accordance with GMP and applicable Law, with replacement or refund at Ono's election.
